chapters.html:
Mydeimos awoke to a hand prodding at his shoulder.

Blearily, he opened his eyes, expression already shaping into a scowl. His vision focused past the harsh sunlight directly above, funneling closer to a figure standing over him.

He had been lying in a field of golden wheat, the wind weaving through the crisp growth in greeting. Mydeimos glared at the boy now before him.

Blue eyes was the first thing he noticed, then the awkward and langley limbs. A boy his age then, growing into a more fitting body. His smile was peculiar, far too pleasant for any occasion.

“You’ll get burned like that,” the boy said.

It was unusual for anyone his age, past those his mother introduced to him, to speak to him. And even those bowed first.

After a moment of silence, the boy spoke again.

“It’s a bit careless to fall asleep under the summer sun.”

Mydeimos’ eye twitched ever so slightly.

“I don’t even know who you are.”

“I’m Phainon,” the boy said, reaching a hand out between them for Mydeimos to take.

Mydeimos stared at that hand, then back up at Phainon, before promptly sitting up and standing on his own. He turned heel, leaving the boy behind him as he began to walk away.

So much for a moment of peace.

Then, after a moment of walking, he heard the rustling of wheat. He looked over his shoulder and saw that boy still following him, that smile still plastered on his face.

“What’s your name?”

Mydeimos bristled, now sensing that this boy was purposefully trying to taunt him. His mother had told him to ignore these sorts of people, and so he did just so.

But the faster he walked, the more it seemed Phainon also quickened his pace. Mydeimos finally whipped around, fully prepared to put an end to this, but was taken aback when he found the boy right in front of him. Phainon put his hands on Mydeimos’ shoulders and playfully shoved him backwards, nearly knocking his balance.

Something akin to embarrassment or anger rose up through his chest at this boy somehow cutting the distance between them and getting the upper hand.

“You-!”

But Phainon just laughed, jumping back a few steps. “Your turn!”

Mydeimos balked. So this was some game?

“You’re not worth my time.”

Phainon narrowed his eyes in challenge, teasing almost. “What? Afraid you won’t be able to catch me?”

. . .

Mydeimos’ fists clenched by his sides, scoffing in disbelief. “Won’t be able to catch you?”

“I’d like to see you try!” Phainon taunted, and then he was off, leaving a trail of trampled wheat in his path as he ran as fast as he could in the opposite direction.

“Hah!” Mydeimos sarcastically laughed, any past notions of decorum his mother taught him gone by the mere bait of a challenge. He immediately took off running, chasing after Phainon.

He admitted that Phainon was faster than most of the children his age, and they had already reached the edge of a forest by the time Mydeimos had caught up. Dashing through lines of splattered trees, Mydeimos eventually grabbed onto the back of Phainon’s brown tunic and tugged him back.

Phainon didn’t seem upset by this though, grinning widely as Mydeimos started running away.

They twisted through the forest, jumping over roots, ducking under branches, sprinting about as fast as they could.

Panting, Mydeimos slowed to a stop. He looked around and didn’t see or hear anything. Blinking, he wondered if he had actually lost Phainon.

Then there was a crunch of leaves to the right, and before Mydeimos could react he was embraced by a pair of arms and thrown over to the ground. The breath was crushed out of him as they landed, and they began rolling together down a hill.

They ended up falling in some shallow creek, and somehow the game had changed over into the two of them wrestling in the water. Mydeimos’ chest and abdomen hurt in a way it hadn’t ever before, and he didn’t understand why until he laughed again. Their voices filled the space, laughter and shouting and taunting.

Finally, Mydeimos managed to flip them over, grabbing Phainon’s wrists and pinning his arms over his head. He was straddled over Phainon’s stomach, squeezing his thighs in so the other couldn’t twist out again.

Phainon was still smiling, despite trying to fight out of Mydeimos’ hold.

“You yield?” Mydeimos panted with a grin, his wet hair dripping down below.

Phainon struggled one last time, before his body finally gave up against the smooth rock base of the creek.

“I yield,” he said, the whites of his teeth showing as he gasped for breath.

Mydeimos finally let go of him, still breathing heavily as he rolled over to lay next to Phainon in the water. He felt the cold rush of it, the creek’s gentle current pulling at his hair and soothing his muscles. He closed his eyes, feeling only the rise and fall of his chest, and the sensation of Phainon beside him.

“That was fun,” Phainon breathily said, and Mydeimos gave a short hum in response.

They laid there in the water for a while longer, until Phainon finally sat up, his backside soaked. He looked down at Mydeimos with a fond gaze.

“You still haven’t told me your name.”

Mydeimos snorted. So he still cared about that.

“It’s —”

“Mydeimos!”

The boys looked up to their right, to the top of the bank. There were two women standing there, both of which Mydeimos was acutely familiar with. One dressed in a simple white chiton, the other with a crimson cape above it and a golden wreath laurel atop her head.

The woman on the left began shuffling down the dirty hillside, scuffing up her sandals in the process of it. Splashing into the water, she helped pull Mydeimos back onto his feet, already worriedly checking him over for any injuries. He endured the process with a bored look in his eyes. He gave a sidelong glance to Phainon, who looked rather confused but still bearing a small smile.

“What were you thinking?” she chastised him, pinching at his arm. “Your mother and I have been looking for you all morning! You think it’s funny now to run off on your own?”

Mydeimos drew his arm back with a moody expression. “I think I can handle myself just fine without you stalking my shadow.”

He was still looking at Phainon instead of the maid.

“Mydeimos.”

A stern, yet warm voice. He finally looked up the bank at his mother.

She held her arms behind her. “Come now. Your swordmaster has been left waiting, and I have much left to do today.”

Mydeimos gave one last glance to Phainon before nodding his head. There was water dripping from his shorter chiton as he walked out of the creek, and he shook his head twice to get his bands out of his eyes. It was a familiar juxtaposition, the feeling of the hot sun against his cooled skin. He took his mother’s extended hand to stand beside her.

The maid came to join beside him, tugging once at the back of his hair as retribution.

“What’s your name, child?” Gorgo asked, giving Phainon a gentle look.

“Phainon, Your Majesty,” Phainon said, bowing his head down despite still being sprawled out in the creek.

Mydeimos looked away to the side. Whatever illusion from before was broken now. He was the crown prince now, and Phainon was just Phainon.

They left soon after going through the pleasantries, though Gorgo seemed to have the ability to connect with just about any of her subjects.

Mydeimos turned his head to look over his shoulder one last time.

Phainon waved to him, mouthing goodbye.

Mydeimos silently lifted a hand as he walked away, watching as Phainon disappeared behind the hill.

~ Mydeimos hadn’t seen Phainon since the week before. Granted, it wasn’t as if he were looking for him. He had spent the last few days just as he did most of his days since coming to this island city. Learning swordplay, fighting with fists, strategy, everything else his mother and her trusted captains knew.

It was afternoon now, Mydeimos seated at the edge of one of the fountains in the inner courtyard of the palace. He was barefoot, sitting with crossed legs as he picked at the platter of food brought out for them. Gorgo was sitting nearby, a foot dipped into the cool pool of water. Mydeimos eyed the mosaic base of the fountain, the small colored tiles smooth and glossy underneath the reflecting light of the water. It was a depiction of a woman fighting a lion. His mother at his age.

It was a quiet day, though Mydeimos could still hear the typical bird song and sounds of the bustling city outside of the palace. Perhaps if he closed his eyes and listened hard enough, he would be able to hear the crashing of waves from the coastline.

This island had not always been his home. For many of the citizens here, it wasn’t home either. They had been living here for the last seven years, settling into life in a new city and trying to create roots. Mydeimos knew, however, that for many, the return home meant more than creating a new life here.

Home was the city of Castrum Kremnos. A shining and vast city surrounding a citadel and palace much larger than this one. For hundreds of years it had thrived alongside its people. Mydeimos still remembered running down those streets as a child, the dances at night festivals, the bustling markets and visitors from afar bringing their cultures.

He still remembered the day Castrum Kremnos was drowned in blood.

Nikador hailed from a neighboring city-state, a war-monger who sought to conquer and rule. Back then, he had only been a crown prince himself. A young man entering his second decade, and yet his years had already been marked in massacre. It was likely, no, certain, that he had already intended to acquire Castrum Kremnos in his possession as well. But perhaps that conquest was hastened by a certain prophecy.

Mydeimos had only heard rumors of it, everyone had only heard rumors of it. After all, Nikador had allegedly labeled any word of it blasphemy punishable by death now that he was a king.

But regardless of this crime, word had spread. That an oracle had prophesied the demise of Nikador. And by no less than the Son of Gorgo, the living Queen of Castrum Kremnos.

He remembered the fires, the blazing arrows and the marching of armies at the depths of night. Gorgo had held his hand as they ran together. They had been ambushed just as they reached the city gates. It was the first and only time Mydeimos had taken a life. He had taken a broken sword from the ground and ran it through a soldier who had meant to cut into his mother. Blood had splattered across his face, the taste of it horrid.

The city had been lost, but Gorgo had led the survivors to a safe haven, an island city belonging to her line of ancestry. They had been hiding here ever since, far away from Nikador’s eyes.

Life had been better since then, though the wounds had never been forgotten. They had rebuilt new lives here under his mother’s leadership and guidance.

But Mydeimos knew what was whispered. That one day they might return home to their kingdom and overthrow the accursed. That justice and retribution would be found, and by the hand of the Son of Gorgo. He knew what the peoples’ eyes held when they looked at him.

Kept secret except for a select few was that Mydeimos had been given a prophecy as well, his fate set out already.

His mother did not speak of this prophecy much, but Mydeimos felt its presence constantly. There was a reason she trained him day in and day out.

There was a reason she taught him strategy, how to rule, how to lead a battle.

It was all for one moment.

Mydeimos fiddled with the figs on his plate, pushing them around.

Gorgo gave him a knowing look. “You were distracted this morning. I’ve never seen you miss your mark like you did today.”

Mydeimos frowned, keeping his eyes low. “It won’t happen again.”

Gorgo hummed. “Distraction in battle has the potential to be the greatest killer. The mind must be focused.”

Embarrassment, and a slight sense of guilt, creeped up on Mydeimos. He knew how much his mother cared. How everyone seemed to care that he grew into something greater than he was.

“I’ll do better,” he said, this time more sincerely.

He could feel her gaze still on him.

“However, sometimes the best way to undo a distraction is to indulge it. Sometimes, that is.”

Mydeimos finally looked up at her.

“You wish to go see your friend?” Gorgo asked.

Mydeimos paused, then looked off to the side, silent. He should have known she would notice.

Gorgo smiled, leaning over to rustle his hair with her fingers. He shook his head about when she was done, attempting to return his hair back to its normal lay.

“Go on then. Be back before dinner.”

Mydeimos nodded, quicker than usual, and Gorgo laughed softly at his reaction.

He didn’t know where Phainon lived, though. He asked a few of the maids, but found they knew no boy of the sorts. And so, with no other options, he went back to that field where they first met.

Today, there were just over two dozen people on the field. Mydeimos frowned, looking out across the land with crossed arms. Everyone here was an adult, hunched over with their sickles as they harvested the wheat. He jumped from the rock he had been standing on, striding over to an older man.

There was the initial forced interaction, the bow and the addressing of Mydeimos as crown prince. Finally, Mydeimos had been able to ask his question, and this time the name was recognized.

“Your Highness wishes to see . . . Phainon?” the old man asked inquisitively.

“Does he live here?” Mydeimos asked.

The old man rubbed the back of his neck, squinting his eyes. “Well, I suppose you could say that. He stays with the livestock out in the stable. Boy’s parents aren’t around anymore, so he works with the animals for a place to sleep and dinner.”

It would explain why Mydeimos had never seen him around the main city. And perhaps explain the overly scrawny limbs.

“Where’s he right now?”

Mydeimos was pointed in the direction of the stable, a decently sized wooden shack with enough space for a dozen or so animals. The front gate was already open, and Mydeimos walked inside without calling out first.

He stopped when he saw a horse with its head out of its pen, rubbing a hand over its nose before moving on. There was someone shuffling in the back of the stable, moving around some buckets and filling them with feed. Mydeimos recognized the lighter head of hair.

The horse snorting beside him gave him away. Phainon turned around, and Mydeimos watched as his expression shifted. Eyes brightening some, a few blinks.

“Didn’t expect to see you here,” he said, standing up and brushing some of the pieces of hay off his knees.

Mydeimos didn’t exactly know what to say, so he just looked back at the horse. She had a roan coat and a star shaped mark across her forehead. He gave her another rub across the nose.

“What’s her name?” he asked.

“Cora.”

She nuzzled against Mydeimos’ head, nibbling some at his hair until he stepped back.

Phainon came to stand by his side, and it was then that Mydeimos noticed the dirt smudged against Phainon’s skin.

They didn’t say anything for a moment.

Then, “If you help me finish in here, I can show you my favorite spot by the cliffs.”

Mydeimos subdued a smile and nodded.

It was likely a curious sight, to see the crown prince working alongside a commoner inside a stable. More than once did Mydeimos catch a head peeking into the stable to watch them. It didn’t take too much longer with the both of them working — feeding the rest of the animals, clearing their pens, and washing their water buckets. By the end of it all the sun was still high in the sky, the both of them walking out of the stable and smelling distinctly of animal fur.

“Come on, it’s this way!” Phainon said, taking off in a jog, and Mydeimos followed alongside him.

Along the way, Phainon was explaining to him how he found the place — apparently last summer when he was chasing after one of the donkeys that got loose. He talked fast, gleefully even. Not once did he use a royal address for Mydeimos.

The spot Phainon wanted to show him was by one of the smaller cliffs by a lagoon. The water there was a pale blue with white rocky shores. There was a sizable tree by the edge of the cliffside, and there tied against one of its larger branches was a rope.

Mydeimos watched as Phainon tested the rope, pulling it taut a few times. Then the boy walked back a few steps, eyes aglow, and sprinted forward. He lifted his legs up, flying up off the cliffside before letting go with a holler, his voice echoing around as he fell down into the water with a tall splash.

Mydeimos jogged over to the side, looking down at the water with wide eyes. He watched as bubbles surfaced up, ripples through the water.

“Phai—!“

The water surface cut open, Phainon popping out with a gasp for breath. He swung his arms around his side, grinning up at Mydeimos.

Mydeimos stared down at him, something relaxing now that he knew the other was safe. Phainon misread his expression.

“Don’t think you can do it?”

It’s all it took for Mydeimos to follow him into the water just the same way, his legs kicking out as he fell through the sky.

The crash into the water was a liminal moment, Phainon’s laughter muffled and the heat of the day disappearing. In the few seconds he was underwater, Mydeimos opened his eyes and looked up.

Sunlight broke through the pool’s surface, dancing through the water in broken reflections. He could see Phainon above him, and Mydeimos began to swim up.

He took a deep breath as he surfaced, blinking his eyes hard to get the water out. Phainon was beside him, face wet and hair flattened on either side of his face. Rosy cheeks, teeth white as ever.

They jumped again and again, one time holding on to the rope and swinging off together. Mydeimos was tired by the time they laid on the rocky shore to rest, muscles sore and exhausted in a way that only felt good.

There had never been anyone for him to play with. The few boys his mother had brought over when he was younger were too forced, somehow always repeating the words their parents had likely forced into their memory the prior night. Every interaction was a constant reminder that he was crown prince.

He didn’t mind that fact. He knew who he was. But it wasn’t everything.

Still, it made him curious why Phainon hadn’t brought it up.

“You haven’t asked about it,” he said, eyes closed. The sun still shone through his eyelids, filling his vision with red.

“About you still smelling like horse?”

Mydeimos smacked a fist against Phainon’s stomach, making the other boy cough out. He opened one eye to look at him.

“About me.”

Phainon was rubbing the place he got hit with a bullied expression. Then he leaned up a little, resting on his forearms so he could look down at Mydeimos better.

“What’s there to ask? I found out when your mother came to fetch you.”

So you didn’t know when you first found me.

“Do you care?” Mydeimos asked. Phainon gave him a funny look, like he thought Mydeimos was joking.

“Do you care?”

Mydeimos stretched out some on the rocks, Phainon’s head blocking the bright rays of the sun. Like this, it was almost as if he were adorning a halo.

“No. I guess not.”

Phainon smiled, reaching over to pluck a stray leaf that had gotten stuck to Mydeimos’ shoulder. He laid it down gently to the side. “Can I ask you something now?”

Mydeimos nodded his head up once.

“Why were you out in the field that day?”

It wasn’t as if that day were truly that special. But it had been the anniversary of sorts from when Mydeimos had first approached the city’s oracle. It had been on his mind that day, after dreaming of those words over and over again.

He had left before anyone could see him, before the breaking of dawn, before any of the maids or teachers could find him. He ran as fast as he could, until he didn’t know where he was. And there he had laid down, closing his eyes and pretending he was far away. Like this was all a dream.

He had managed to pretend it was until Phainon had woken him.

“I had a lot on my mind,” is what he opted to say instead.

Phainon gave him an oddly knowing smile. “Sure.”

Mydeimos blinked slowly. “And why are you working on the farm? Your parents?”

He asked it despite knowing the answer. He didn’t know why, but he wanted to hear it from Phainon himself.

“Why should I give you an answer when you didn’t?”

Mydeimos’ brows scrunched up. “I gave you an answer.”

“‘I had a lot on my mind’ doesn’t count as an answer,” Phainon snorted, tugging at the skirt of Mydeimos’ chiton.

Mydeimos huffed, putting an arm down so he could sit up as well. He gave Phainon a sideways glance. His mother would advise him to be careful who he sought counsel from. He found he didn’t really care about that right now.

“You know about Nikador’s prophecy, right?”

Even someone like Phainon, who didn’t seem that caught up in city gossip, should know about it.

“My mother mentioned it once, back in the day.”

Phainon sat up fully beside him. “Something about the Son of Gorgo being the one to kill him.”

Mydeimos looked out at the water again. It was an uneasy feeling, one he liked to pretend didn’t exist.

“A year ago I saw the oracle. I got my own prophecy.”

He couldn’t see Phainon’s expression, but could hear him shifting slightly. The boy was waiting for him to continue before speaking.

“It . . . It wasn’t anything different,” he said flatly. “It was the exact same. I’ll be the one to kill him.”

The oracle had laughed after she had told him.

You see, fate has its way of balancing the scales.

“I guess I was just thinking about it.”

It was a strange shift of mood, given what this started out as. Two boys, perhaps not yet friends, lying beside each other after an hour of play.

Phainon tucked his head over his knees, looking up at Mydeimos.

“And you’re afraid?”

His words weren’t meant to be mocking, nor were they in humor. He meant it just as that, as if he had known from the first day they had met that Mydeimos had been afraid. It took Mydeimos off guard.

“I . . .”

Mydeimos licked the back of his teeth. A habit he had picked up.

“There’s nothing to be afraid of. It’s a good thing.”

“It is a good thing. But that doesn’t mean it isn’t heavy. It doesn’t mean you can’t be afraid of it.”

Mydeimos finally turned to look at Phainon. His eyes were as blue as the water ahead of them.

“Do you think prophecies have to be true?” Mydeimos asked after a moment.

Phainon took a breath.

“Yes. I do.”

It was the answer Mydeimos had expected. All prophecies came to fruition, no matter their words.

“But what matters is the journey we take to that end,” Phainon said. “You may be afraid of your prophecy today, Mydeimos. But I assure you. One day you won’t be. You’ll face it with your head held high.”

How can you say that with such conviction?

Mydeimos wiped some of the water off his face with the back of his hand. “Maybe.”

Phainon gave a quick smile, grabbing a nearby rock and tossing it into the lagoon. “Alright, I owe you an answer now.”

Thankful that the topic of conversation had moved away from himself, Mydeimos turned to pay attention.

He spoke like he was talking about the weather, and Mydeimos began to wonder if Phainon was just as secretive as himself, though perhaps in a different way.

“My folks died several years back. My mother was in the army when Nikador invaded Castrum Kremnos, I heard she died near the end when we were evacuating. Father and I lived here together for another two years before he died. He got sick one day and just didn’t get better.”

Phainon threw another rock, and this time it skipped across the water. “Loukas, the owner of the farm, found me sleeping in the stables with the horses. I somehow convinced him to let me stay, though I have to work to keep my spot.”

He shrugged. “It’s not so bad. The old man treats me well, and so does the rest of the workers who come around. We’re not family, but we get along.”

Mydeimos tipped his head to the side. “Do you miss them?”

Phainon glanced at him, smiling. “Yeah.”

Death was a strange thing.

He didn’t know what prompted him to say it, and it was as if he really hadn’t thought of it before the words slipped out.

“You know, you could come live with me instead.”

Phainon raised his brow in question.

“We have plenty of rooms.”

The other boy laughed. “You invite everyone you meet to come live with you?”

Mydeimos didn’t think it would bode so well to admit that he had probably spoken more willing words to Phainon than anyone else his age.

He scowled instead. “What? You’d rather live in the stables?”

Phainon flicked him on his forehead. “Plenty of people live in worse. I consider myself quite lucky.”

Mydeimos didn’t really understand, but Phainon seemed rather stubborn about it.

“I like being independent,” Phainon explained in the silence Mydeimos had left. “It feels good to be living off my own work.”

“You could still work there if you wanted,” Mydeimos grumbled. “You just wouldn’t have to sleep on the ground anymore.”

Again, he couldn’t understand why he was persisting.

Phainon bit the inside of his cheek as if he were mulling it over. Then, he spoke.

“You know, you’re nicer than I thought.”

Mydeimos glared daggers at him, to no avail.

“I have to spend the harvesting season here. It’s easier for me to wake up and already be at work,” Phainon explained casually. “After that, I’ll consider your offer. That is, as long as you aren’t tired of me by then.”

Somehow, it felt like another challenge. Mydeimos nodded in agreement.

The two of them headed back to the farm not so long after that. They walked this time, limbs sore from swimming and jumping into the water.

Halfway back, Phainon stopped to pluck a vibrant yellow wildflower from the ground. He rotated it about between his thumb and index finger before coming and tucking it behind Mydeimos’ ear.

Mydeimos scoffed, pulling it out and throwing it back down as Phainon laughed beside him.

~

Just before the end of the harvest season, Mydeimos had brought Phainon to the baths with him. Phainon had initially rejected the offer, given how much work there was to be done, but he found that Loukas had nervously insisted he take the day off. He had a creeping feeling that Mydeimos had done some sort of bribery, or threatening, to get his way.

Regardless, he had finally accepted, following along as Mydeimos showed him the way through town. He hadn’t been before, which Mydeimos seemed to inwardly enjoy. They washed themselves ahead in a cold bath, which Phainon was used to, but he was fully unprepared for the almost suffocating heat of the thermal bath room. Steam was rising from the murky waters, a distinct lavender scent curling around their bodies.

Mydeimos had picked one of the more private baths in the city, and there weren’t too many others there. With the steam, Phainon could only make out the vague shape of upper bodies in the water.

He looked down at his bare feet as they walked through the room, padding across colored mosaics of sea creatures and ships. It was a beautiful sight, and Phainon was almost taken aback by how casually Mydeimos walked over them without looking down.

‘Though I suppose he must be used to this,’ Phainon thought.

He walked a little faster to catch up to Mydeimos’ side.

They picked one of the pools in the back of the room where they’d be alone. The milky water was littered with flower petals, steam hazy as it floated upwards.

Experimentally, Phainon leaned down to dip his hand into the pool.

He immediately tore his hand back with a jump, not expecting the water to be so hot. Mydeimos laughed at him, walking straight into the scorching water without hesitation. His towel was thrown unceremoniously to the side of the pool, without any shame.

Mydeimos gave a goading smile, dipping down into the water until it came up to his chest.

“I didn’t know you couldn’t handle the heat,” he mocked.

Phainon’s eyes shined, and he dipped his hand back into the water. His skin stung, likely turning a little pink, but he figured it was worth it.

He noticed how the ends of Mydeimos’ hair dipped into the water, and finally he began stepping inside. His face must have been scrunched up at the way Mydeimos continued to grin, and he let out a hiss as he finally lowered his torso into the water. It took several moments before he could relax into the water, finally feeling the sensation of tense muscles releasing. It was surprising how pleasant it felt on his sore feet and back. He wondered if Mydeimos had brought him here knowing that.

They swam, or rather waded through the water for some time, speaking in low voices so as to not disturb the others.

Mydeimos was, as expected, interesting to talk to. To Phainon, he was someone who had lived a thousand lives, despite them being the same age.

And yet Mydeimos asked him the same amount of questions, seemingly interested in Phainon’s opinions on various topics, from whatever situation at home was troubling Mydeimos to local politics, even about the ending of some book which Mydeimos had summarized the entirety of to him.

“You know,” Phainon eventually said. “With your hair so long, you could braid it. Try it.”

He wasn’t entirely sure what prompted such a thought, but his eyes had been lingering at Mydeimos’ hair for some time now. He had some bangs and pieces cropped to frame his face, but otherwise his hair reached his shoulders in the front.

Mydeimos snorted. “Why would I know how to do that?”

Phainon exhaled in exasperation, swimming a little closer to Mydeimos. “It’s not hard.”

It’s not like he had his own hair to demonstrate, so he pulled the three locks from Mydeimos’ hair. He gave a verbal description, though he was sure Mydeimos wouldn’t actually remember.

“Like that,” he finished, holding the small braid together with his fingers. It was just by Mydeimos’ ear, but it looked just as Phainon had imagined. “Looks good.”

The blood there was warm, staining against both their hands and creeping into the lines of their skin.

“I’m here, I’m here,” Phainon kept whispering, crying. “Mydeimos, I’m here.”

Mydeimos gazed at him, touching at Phainon’s hand.

The pain now, the wounds and the poison, was becoming numb.

Weakly, and silently, he shook his head.

And after a few seconds, Phainon’s shaking hands finally let him go.

Their eyes met.

He knew then that Phainon would understand.

Just hold me now.

“Phainon,” Mydeimos murmured. “You came back.”

Warmth. How warm Phainon was beside him.

There was a smile then, though it didn’t quite reach Phainon’s eyes. His voice was fragile, a frayed line about to snap. And Mydeimos knew that Phainon was trying to be strong for him at this moment.

“I couldn’t leave you.”

Mydeimos swallowed, his tongue heavy. So many words to say, and yet life was seeping out of him. He was so tired.

The price of prophecy.

And yet he was no longer afraid. The end was here, after so many years.

All there was now, was them.

“It’s okay,” Phainon whispered softly. “You don’t need to say anything. I understand.”

The man shifted so they could look easier at one another, and Mydeimos’ gaze softened. The blue of Phainon’s eyes were paler in this light, the lines of his face just as Mydeimos remembered them. He traced them all, just as he had done so many times before.

How clear those memories were, when there was nothing except for them in the world.

“It’s okay,” Phainon said, his voice warbling. “I’m here. I’m going to take care of you, Mydeimos. I promise you.”

Mydeimos blinked slowly, dark clouds beginning to haze over his field of vision. All he could see now was Phainon, whose features even now were blurring. In fading recognition, Mydeimos watched as Phainon fought back his tears. The strain of his lips, throat held tight, the inner corner of his brows raised in such a way.

He grasped as tightly as he could onto Phainon’s hand, though his fingers had barely any strength left. Yet Phainon still lifted their hands up together, fingers interwoven as he kissed the back of Mydeimos’ knuckles.

“Won’t you . . .” Mydeimos quietly began to speak, voice hoarse. Phainon leaned in closer to hear him.

“Forgive me?”

At the end of all things.

Phainon was still for a moment, and all Mydeimos saw was the wind which caught Phainon’s hair in its breeze. Then, the feeling of wetness dripping onto his cheeks. Phainon’s tears.

The man nodded once, twice.

“I forgive you, Mydeimos. I am with you. I will always be with you.”

Mydeimos tried to part his lips, but his voice was gone. His blood pooled out on the tiles below, so dark in the harsh sunlight it was almost black.

For there were words unsaid. Words he had never uttered, despite how deeply he had harbored them.

It was as if he were forgetting how to breathe, and he felt himself choking on the very air.

Mydeimos took their intertwined hands and pulled them to his chest, laying them across his heart.

Everything he wished to say, with the beat of his heart slowing now.

Phainon squeezed his fingers, nodding. He leaned closer, pressing his lips against Mydeimos’ cheek, his lips. Those words once again, those words Mydeimos had once been too cowardly to say back.

“Phainon,” Mydeimos wished to whisper into his skin. “I love you.”

His eyelids fell as he tilted his face one last time to feel Phainon there beside him.

To stay like this forever.

There was a touch. And Mydeimos finally fell still.

Phainon waited until he was sure, until Mydeimos was no longer there. He kissed the man’s brow, chest constricting as tears stained down his cheeks.

He whispered his name, over and over again, as if time could turn back. Reality blurred, memories coming in waves, and Phainon could hear the shores of the sea. Mydeimos’ eyes were closed, and his expression at peace.

In the distance, the sound of clattering armor and marching. Their battle had ended. The army was beginning to crest over the hill, to come to their triumphant and fallen king.

Phainon paid them no heed, instead looking down upon Mydeimos and the golden sunlight which scattered across his skin. It was as if he were asleep, just like that day Phainon had first found him.

And Mydeimos was there now, in that liminal space of memory.

He wept, and softly, tenderly, pressed their foreheads together one last time.

I will fulfill my promise to you. I will lead our people home. I will have your name etched into history.

Dream of me the way I will dream of you.

And one day, I will follow you again into those endless fields of gold.
